      <description><p>At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports</p><p>Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a <a href="https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/10/12/senegal-brutal-crackdown-violates-lgbt-peoples-rights">new report</a>.</p><p>More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, <a href="https://www.hivjustice.net/cases/senegal-crackdown-on-lgbtq-people-intensifies-with-multiple-arrests/">according to HIV Justice Network</a>, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/oct/15/senegal-homosexuality-criminalised-anti-lgbtq-arrests-hiv-testing-human-rights-watch">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next </p><p>A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.</p><p>Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors, of varying popularity, gazed disinterestedly at the scene.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-interactive/2026/oct/18/4000-people-minding-our-own-business-four-decades-on-falklands-again-face-a-hostile-argentina">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2026/oct/18/michael-gove-justifies-his-politics-radical-thinking-with-aditya-chakrabortty</link>
      <description><p>For more than three decades, <strong>Michael Gove</strong> has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins <strong>Aditya Chakrabortty</strong> to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam</p><p>Watch the full episode with Michael Gove <a href="https://youtu.be/cIGXagkUFr8">here</a>.
 <br>
 <br>
 Aditya’s suggested reading:</p><p>To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today<em> </em>gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair</p><p>For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, read <a href="https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v41/n17/richard-j.-evans/the-demented-dalek">The Demented Dalek</a> by the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books</p><p>To learn more on what’s become of the British right, there’s a Guardian <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2024/sep/12/tory-leadership-jenrick-tugendhat-cleverly-badenoch">column by Aditya </a></p><p>Phil Burton-Cartledge analyses in depth why the most successful political party is now failing in his book <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/the-partys-over-9781839760372/">The Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak</a></p><p>Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshall a coalition of voters. <a href="https://averypublicsociologist.blogspot.com/2026/10/the-clear-blue-water-strategy.html">Here</a> he is on Kemi Badenoch</p><p>Geoffrey Wheatcroft does an entertaining short narrative in <a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/bloody-panico-9781804295755/">Bloody Panico!:</a></p><p><a href="https://guardianbookshop.com/bloody-panico-9781804295755/">or, Whatever Happened to The Tory Party</a></p><p>For more on the economics of the Cameron years, <a href="https://foundationaleconomy.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/wp87.pdf">this paper</a> is acute on how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series.</p><p>And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, there’s <a href="https://www.nber.org/papers/w34459?st_source=ai_overview">this paper</a> based on data from the Bank of England</p><p>Finally, on the Spectator, read Nesrine Malik’s recent Guardian column</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/jul/20/islamophobia-spectator-britain-oldest-political-magazine">Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia?</a></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2026/oct/18/michael-gove-justifies-his-politics-radical-thinking-with-aditya-chakrabortty">Continue reading...</a></description>
